PRESCHOOL · AGE 3 · CLASS 3 MAGIC GAME

Magic Shape Builder

Five pictures are waiting to be built from shapes. Start with a three-shape house, then a tree, a rocket, a butterfly — and finally the big seven-shape robot. Tap a piece, tap its spot, and watch the picture appear. Grown-ups read the words; little ones do the building.

No scores, no timers — just building.

CHOOSE A DESIGN

What shall we build first?

The house is the easiest — three shapes. Every picture you finish unlocks the next one. You can rebuild any picture as many times as you like.

Finishing a picture unlocks the next one — and your builds are remembered on this device.

OFF-SCREEN PLAY

Shapes you can hold.

The best shape set costs nothing: cut, sort and stack with what you already have. Pick one of these and let your child lead.

Paper shape cutouts

  • Cut circles, squares, triangles and rectangles from paper or old magazines — then rebuild the house or the rocket on the table, just like on the screen.

Household shape hunt

  • Build a picture from household objects: a plate circle, a book rectangle, a corner triangle. Photograph the result for your own art wall.

Snack shapes

  • Crackers, banana slices and cheese triangles are building materials too. Build, name each shape, then eat the architecture.

One safety word for this game: grown-ups handle scissors for the cutouts, and snack builds use foods your child already eats safely — cut grapes small, and sit down together to build and munch.

ACTIVITY COMPLETE

Shapes in all the right places!

Circles, squares, rectangles, triangles and ovals are now your child’s building blocks — on the screen, on the table and around the house. Whether you built one picture or all five, that was real shape practice, and there was never a score to worry about.

FOR GROWN-UPS

How building teaches shapes.

Each board is drawn to match its reference picture: the same shapes, in the same places, one empty spot at a time. The current spot is big, outlined in the color of the piece that belongs there, and labeled with its shape word — so a child always knows where the next piece goes and can spend their attention on which piece that is. A piece only clicks into the spot that matches both its shape and its color; a wrong tap gets a gentle sentence, never a buzz, and after two tries the board quietly points at the piece that fits.

The builds grow with your child: the house is three shapes, the robot is seven, and each finished picture unlocks the next. Finished builds are remembered on this device only — nothing is uploaded, and no name is attached. The reference picture stays beside every board on purpose: comparing the picture with the work-in-progress is the actual skill — looking carefully, checking, trying again.

Tap-to-place works with mouse, touch and keyboard: pieces and the current spot are real buttons, and dragging works too. And the paper-cutout version in Off-Screen Play is where the shapes become something your child can hold.
